title: Quantum multi-label k-nearest neighbor
abstract: Although multi-label k-nearest neighbor (ML-kNN) is able to effectively solve multi-label learning (MLL) problem with local neighborhood similarity, its time complexity is nearly unacceptable with large-scale datasets. To solve this issue, we propose a novel ML-kNN algorithm with quantum computing techniques, which called quantum multi-label k-nearest neighbor (QML-kNN). In particular, we first accelerate the calculation of the prior probability by taking advantage of quantum phase estimation and Grover's amplitude amplification. Then, a controlled-SWAP test and a quantum k-maximal similarity search are used for efficiently identifying the neighbors. Subsequently, a quantum parallel counting circuit (QPCC) is designed to rapidly calculate the posterior probabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that QML-kNN is able to significantly reduce the time complexity of solving multi-label problems with performance improvement, achieving a substantial speedup over the classical MLL algorithm.
summary: This paper introduces QML-kNN, a quantum algorithm designed to overcome the computational bottleneck of traditional ML-kNN for multi-label classification. By utilizing quantum circuits for probability estimation and neighbor searching, it achieves significant theoretical speedups and superior performance compared to its classical counterpart.
main_problem: The classical Multi-label k-Nearest Neighbor (ML-kNN) algorithm suffers from unacceptable time complexity when applied to large-scale, high-dimensional datasets.
main_result: The proposed Quantum ML-kNN (QML-kNN) significantly reduces the time complexity and outperforms classical methods across all tested evaluation metrics.
method: It integrates quantum techniques—including quantum counting circuits, c-SWAP tests, and a specialized Quantum Parallel Counting Circuit (QPCC)—to accelerate probability estimation and neighbor searching.
model_or_system: The model is an algorithmic framework designed to replace classical ML-kNN steps with quantum subroutines. These include using Quantum Phase Estimation for prior probabilities and amplitude encoding/c-SWAP tests for similarity calculation.
key_observables: Hamming Loss, Coverage, Ranking Loss, One-error, Macro-AUC, and computational time complexity (Big O notation).
important_parameters: Feature dimension ($U$), training instances ($m$), number of neighbors ($k$), and number of labels ($Q$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on theoretical models for quantum speedups; practical implementation is currently limited by existing quantum hardware.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall QML-kNN workflow across three modules, show performance comparisons between classical and quantum approaches (e.g., Fig. 8), and plot the leading-order complexity reduction achieved by the quantum algorithm (e.g., Fig. 9).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of ML-kNN. It then details the QML-kNN framework across three modules: Module A for prior probabilities using QPE/Grover's, Module B for neighbor search via c-SWAP and quantum k-maximal search, and Module C for posterior probability calculation using a QPCC.
why_interesting: It demonstrates a direct application of advanced quantum algorithms (QAE, Quantum Counting) to solve a complex machine learning problem, providing concrete theoretical speedups that could motivate hardware development in the NISQ era.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. An example of the ML-kNN algorithm. The dataset contains 23 instances, each possibly associated with up to three labels e, f, g given in the legend. The circle marks the k = 10 nearest neighbors of the central instance x.
FIG. 2. Overall workflow of QML-kNN. It is divided into prior probability calculation, quantum k-nearest neighbor search and posterior probability calculation.
FIG. 3. Quantum counting circuit for calculating Ml. It mainly integrates controlled Grover iterations with IQFT, starting from a uniform superposition of all training instances.
FIG. 4. Circuit for the c-SWAP test. It consists of two Hadamard gates and a SWAP gate that exchanges the two input states when the control qubit is |1⟩.

FIG. 5. The quantum circuit for QAE. QAA process converts the probability information associated with the amplitudes into corresponding phase information, which is subsequently extracted by the QPE procedure.
